pages.title: Why use the Copilot app
pages.caption: Copilot in your editor or terminal is great next to the code you have open. The hard part is supervising agent work end to end. The app doesn’t replace your editor. It’s one desktop control center to run and review that work: **project sessions** keep focused work separate, sessions, diffs, terminal output, previews and GitHub work sit in **one app**, **chats** are for safe questions, **canvases** give you and the agent a shared board in the side panel, and **Automations** save a prompt you’d otherwise retype.

pages.title: Keep your editor
pages.caption: Keep VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains or your usual editor for deep editing. From the app, you can open the same project in VS Code any time you want a full editor.

pages.title: New
pages.caption: The landing view. Start a chat without a project, pick a connected project for a project session, choose a mode and model, or start from one of the suggested prompts.

pages.title: Pull requests
pages.caption: Lists the GitHub pull requests that involve you. Tabs such as **Authored by me** and **Review requests** filter the list. To limit it to one repository, use the filter icon and a `repo:OWNER/REPOSITORY` query (Chapter 03 shows the steps). Open a pull request to read its checks and comments, or start a session to work on it. The practice pull requests from setup are on the **Authored by me** tab.

pages.title: Issues
pages.caption: The same idea for GitHub issues, with tabs such as **Assigned to me** and **Created by me**. Start a session from an issue, or select **New issue** to create one. The practice issues from setup are assigned to you, so they’re on the **Assigned to me** tab.

pages.title: Dashboards
pages.caption: Your GitHub work as a board of widgets: small panels that each show a filtered list, so you can see what needs your attention without opening each list. The default **My Work** dashboard has **Pulls created**, **Pulls mentioned**, **Issues assigned**, **Issues mentioned** and **Requested reviews**. The practice items from setup are in **Pulls created** and **Issues assigned**.

pages.title: Automations
pages.caption: Recurring agent tasks. The view shows templates that run manually, daily or weekly, and automations can also be triggered by events. You choose local or cloud execution when you set one up. Chapter 07 covers automations.

pages.title: Customize
pages.caption: Where you manage the ways to extend the app: skills, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, plugins, extensions and canvases. You don’t need any yet. Chapter 04 covers skills and custom agents, Chapter 05 MCP servers and plugins, and Chapter 06 canvases.

pages.title: Sessions and chats
pages.caption: The **Sessions** area of the sidebar lists every project you’ve connected. Start your first chat, and a **Chats** row shows up there too.

pages.title: Chats and project sessions
pages.caption: A **chat session** is for asking, brainstorming, summarizing and getting your bearings, and it doesn’t create a branch or worktree. A **project session** is for planning, inspecting, editing, testing or making PR-ready work, and usually creates one, depending on session settings.

pages.title: In the control room
pages.caption: A producer doesn’t handle every song the same way. Some quick questions just need a fast answer, some takes need close direction, and some need the arrangement charted first. The app works the same way: first choose the kind of session, then a mode for how closely you direct the work.

pages.title: Start a chat
pages.caption: Select **+** next to **Sessions**, then **Chat**. Check that the project picker below the prompt box shows **Chat**, then send the prompt. The reply should say chats suit general questions and project sessions bring repository context. It shouldn’t change any files, and the app doesn’t create a branch or worktree for a chat.
pages.code: In the GitHub Copilot app, explain when I should use a chat and when I should use a project session. Do not create or change files.

pages.title: Tour the sample in a project session
pages.caption: Use a project session when the agent needs your repository, changes code or makes something like a pull request. Most project sessions should use a **New worktree**. Chapter 00’s setup session on **Current checkout** was the exception. The app remembers that choice for your next session, so you’ll switch back to **New worktree** in Chapter 02. Return to the setup session, listed under `copilot-app-for-beginners` in the sidebar, and send this. The reply should cover `samples/book-app-web`’s purpose, technologies, main files, data flow and tests, and change nothing.
pages.code: I'm learning the copilot-app-for-beginners course. Give me a beginner-friendly tour of the samples/book-app-web sample before I begin the hands-on exercises. Explain what the app does, the technologies it uses, how its main files are organized, how data flows through it and what the tests cover. Refer to specific file paths and finish with a suggested reading order. Do not change any files.

pages.title: Interactive, Plan and Autopilot
pages.caption: **Interactive**: step-by-step collaboration, for when you want to be involved throughout. **Plan**: plan first, execute when ready, for when the approach and details matter. **Autopilot**: end-to-end execution without interruption, for well-defined tasks with clear outcomes. Pick the mode that fits the task. The mode menu also has **Tool permissions**: **Always ask** asks before each tool, **Approve all** runs tools without asking, and **Assisted** asks only when a tool request fails an AI safety check.

pages.title: Model and reasoning effort
pages.caption: The model control sits below the prompt box, next to the mode selector, and shows **Copilot Fusion** or a model name. With an individual model, open it for **Model**, **Effort** and **Context window**. With **Copilot Fusion**, it shows an **Effort level** instead. The context window is how much text the model can hold at once; a larger one can help long sessions or large codebases, but can use more AI credits. For a tour or a short explanation, use **Copilot Fusion** at **Standard**, or keep your current model and its default effort. For a hard bug or a change across several files, consider a higher Fusion effort level or a model suited to complex coding. Higher effort doesn’t guarantee a correct answer. If a response doesn’t work for you, select **Retry** below it to try again with a different model, effort or context window, without retyping your prompt.

pages.title: Copilot Fusion
pages.caption: **Copilot Fusion** is in the model control, but it isn’t a single model. It selects models and a workflow for each request, then returns one response: it can use one model, ask a stronger model to improve a draft, or ask another model to review the result. It isn’t **Autopilot**: Fusion controls how models handle your request, and Autopilot controls how independently the agent works. Turn off the **Copilot Fusion** switch to choose an individual model. Its effort levels: **Standard** for everyday coding tasks (start here for this course), **High** for challenging tasks, and **Max** for the most demanding ones. Higher levels can take longer and use more AI credits. They don’t guarantee a correct result, so keep reviewing changes and running tests. Availability depends on your app version, plan and organization policy.

pages.title: Try the controls
pages.caption: In your project session, select **Interactive** mode. Open the model control: if **Copilot Fusion** is selected, keep **Standard**. Otherwise, use **Model** to select an available model, and keep the default effort. Then send this. The reply should say search matches titles and authors whatever the letter case, and point to `samples/book-app-web/src/App.tsx`. You can change the model and effort mid-session without changing the mode.
pages.code: In samples/book-app-web, explain how filterBooks searches book titles and authors. Does letter case affect the results? Refer to the relevant file. Do not change any files.

pages.title: The Model Market
pages.caption: Models differ in capabilities, speed and usage cost. For a repository tour or a short explanation, use **Copilot Fusion** at **Standard**, or keep your current model and its default reasoning effort. For a difficult bug or a change across several files, consider a higher Fusion effort level or a model suited to complex coding, though higher effort doesn’t guarantee a correct answer. If a response doesn’t work for you, select **Retry** below it to try again with a different model or effort, without retyping your prompt. (Gilda’s boards group the models the way GitHub Docs does: Lightweight, Versatile and Powerful. Copilot Fusion is her house special.)

pages.title: Prompts and shortcuts
pages.caption: You’ll type most prompts in the composer box below the session. Press **{key:mod+R}** to see your recent prompts across all sessions: search them, and select one to reuse it. Type `@` to attach files and folders, `#` for issues and pull requests, and `/` to run commands.

pages.title: Settings
pages.caption: Select the gear at the bottom of the sidebar to open **Settings**. **General**: updates, where repositories are stored, the theme. **Accounts**: add another GitHub account. **Sessions**: manage sessions and chats, response style, app-wide instructions, branch naming. **Themes**: pick and customize the app theme. **Accessibility**: zoom, keyboard shortcuts, notifications. **Voice dictation**: microphone, shortcut, transcription models. **Customize**: points you to the **Customize** view. **Model providers**: your own API keys (it doesn’t replace the model picker). **Experimental**: preview features. **Repositories**: per-repository settings, such as **Show in sidebar**, sandbox rules and the default branch.

pages.title: Voice dictation (optional)
pages.caption: Voice dictation turns speech into editable prompt text, and it’s on by default. In **Settings**, select **Voice dictation** to set up your input device, and change the microphone or transcription model if you need to. Under **Microphone privacy**, select **Open preferences** to allow the microphone in your operating system, then select **Test mic** and note the shortcut. Then start a new chat (**+** next to **Sessions**, then **Chat**) and try the shortcut.

pages.title: Next: Chapter 02
pages.caption: Chapter 02 solves the “shared working copy” challenge: isolated sessions with worktrees, plus focused context with `@`, `#` and `/`. [Continue to Chapter 02 ↗](https://github.com/github/copilot-app-for-beginners/blob/main/02-sessions-worktrees-context/README.md)

pages.title: I can’t find a setting
pages.caption: Settings vary by app version, operating system, organization policy and enabled features. Look for the closest matching category, then check the official docs if the screen still doesn’t match.

pages.title: Voice dictation doesn’t work
pages.caption: Check microphone permission, whether the local transcription model has downloaded, shortcut conflicts, and language support.

pages.title: A mode or model is missing
pages.caption: Check your plan, your organization’s policy, your project settings and your app version. Available models and effort levels vary, and some models don’t offer an effort setting.

glossary.definition: A session for questions and brainstorming. It doesn’t create a branch or worktree.
The sidebar view that lists the pull requests that involve you, with tabs such as Authored by me and Review requests.
The sidebar view that lists the issues that involve you, with tabs such as Assigned to me and Created by me.
The sidebar view that shows your GitHub work as a board of widgets, each a filtered list, such as Pulls created and Issues assigned.
Saved agent tasks that run on demand, on a schedule, or from selected GitHub events.
Where you manage skills, MCP servers, plugins, extensions and canvases.
Interactive (step by step), Plan (plan first, execute when ready) and Autopilot (end to end without interruption).
In the mode menu: whether the agent asks before it uses a tool. Always ask, Approve all, or Assisted (asks only when a request fails an AI safety check).
A model-control option that selects models and a workflow for each request, then returns one response. It isn’t a single model or a session mode. Its effort levels are Standard, High and Max.
How much reasoning a supported model uses. Higher can help with complex problems but takes longer.
How much text the model can hold at once, including the conversation and the files it reads. Larger can help long sessions but uses more AI credits.

The app’s options, opened with the gear at the bottom of the sidebar: General, Accounts, Sessions, Themes, Accessibility, Voice dictation, Customize, Model providers, Experimental, and each repository’s own settings under Repositories.
A setting that connects models from other providers with your own API keys.

P1.1.bug.text: Fixing a bug changes code in your repository. That needs a project session.

P1.1.brainstorm.text: Brainstorming is exploring. A chat makes no branch or worktree, and it doesn’t need one.

P1.1.test.text: Adding a test edits code in your repository. That’s project work.

P1.1.worktree.text: That’s a general question. It doesn’t need your repository, so ask it in a chat.

P1.1.pr.text: A pull request is made from your repository. Start a project session.

P1.1.tour.text: No files change, but it needs your repository. That’s a project session.

market.quote.autopilot.text: Copilot Fusion is different from **Autopilot**. Fusion controls how models handle your request. Autopilot controls how independently the agent works.

market.quote.autoLevels.text: These levels guide Copilot Fusion's model choices. They are not the reasoning settings of one fixed model.

market.quote.autoMore.text: Higher levels can take longer and use more AI credits.
